opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think programming contests were a really useful proving ground for a while because they have a lot of nice properties. The problems are well-specified, there's an objective grader, and there's a large population of strong humans to compare against. So you get a clean signal. But once models are performing at or near the top of those leaderboards, the signal starts to saturate, and you have to ask what you were actually trying to measure in the first place.

For me, what we really care about is whether models can do useful, open-ended work, the kind of thing a strong researcher or engineer does over days or weeks rather than in a three-hour window. Contest problems are self-contained and short-horizon. Real work is messy. You have to figure out what the problem even is, deal with ambiguous requirements, navigate a large existing codebase, recover from your own mistakes, and decide when something is good enough. So one direction is evaluations that stretch the time horizon: tasks that take a human expert many hours, where you measure not just whether the model gets there but how reliably it does.

A second direction is moving toward evaluations grounded in real economic or scientific value. Can the model resolve actual issues in real repositories? Can it reproduce a research paper's results? Can it make a novel contribution that experts agree is meaningful? Those are harder to grade, and that's the crux of it: as capabilities go up, grading becomes the bottleneck. You can't always write a unit test for "did this produce a genuinely good research idea." So I think we'll lean more on expert human judgment, on carefully designed rubrics, and increasingly on models helping evaluate other models, with a lot of care about where that can go wrong.

Third, I'd emphasize reliability and robustness over peak performance. A model that solves a hard problem once in a hundred tries is interesting, but a model that solves a moderately hard problem ninety-nine times out of a hundred is often much more useful. Evals should capture that distribution, not just the best case.

And finally, there's the question of contamination and Goodhart's law. Any benchmark that becomes popular eventually gets optimized against, directly or indirectly. So I think the field needs a steady supply of fresh, held-out evaluations, and honestly a bit of humility. The best evaluation in the end is whether people find the models genuinely useful in their own work, and whether the models help push the frontier of knowledge forward. Contests were a great milestone, but they were always a proxy for that.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think programming contests were great for a while because they gave us a very clean signal. There's a right answer, there's a time limit, you can verify it automatically, and the problems are hard enough that progress on them actually meant something. But I think we've kind of saturated that. Once you have a model that's performing at the level of the top handful of humans in the world on Codeforces or IOI-style problems, the benchmark stops telling you much. It becomes a ceiling effect, and honestly it stops being that representative of the work we actually want these models to do.

So the direction I think evaluation needs to go is toward long-horizon, open-ended tasks that look a lot more like real work. A competitive programming problem is maybe thirty minutes to a couple of hours of focused effort with a crisp spec. Real software engineering is: here's a messy codebase, here's an ambiguous request from a product manager, go figure out what the right thing to build is, build it, test it, deal with the fact that the environment is flaky, and come back in a week. There's no single ground truth, and a lot of the value is in judgment, not just raw problem-solving.

That makes evaluation much harder for a few reasons. One is verification. When there's no clean answer key you either need human experts to grade, which is slow and expensive and noisy, or you need models to grade, and then you have to worry about whether the grader is reliable and whether you're just measuring agreement with another model's biases. I think a lot of the interesting work right now is in building rubrics and process-based evals that let you check intermediate steps rather than just the final output.

Another is that the tasks need to measure things we actually care about and that we can't get from static benchmarks. Can the model stay on task over thousands of steps? Does it know when to ask for clarification versus when to just make a reasonable call? Does it notice when it's wrong and recover? Does it do the thing you asked or does it quietly do something easier? Those are the properties that determine whether a model is useful as an agent, and contests don't probe them at all.

And then the third thing is that I think we need to move toward evals that are closer to scientific or economically meaningful output. Can a model make a genuine contribution to a research problem? Can it run an experiment end to end? Those are the kinds of capabilities that matter for the next phase, and we should be building evaluations that are honest about how far along we are rather than ones that make us feel good because the score went up.

The last point I'd make is that as models get more capable, evaluation becomes less about finding out what they can do and more about finding out where they break. The failure modes get subtler. So I think evaluation has to become more adversarial, more about stress testing and red-teaming for reliability, and less about leaderboards. The leaderboard was the right tool for a certain era. I don't think it's the right tool for where we're going.

r001.rationale: It proposes evaluations of genuine research contributions and end-to-end experiments, explicitly moving evaluation toward scientific output.

r002.rationale: It does not identify coding coworking or describe testing whether models learn in high-context settings.

r003.rationale: It discusses long-horizon real-world software tasks, but does not identify coding coworking as a test of models learning in those settings.

astra-6.text:
I think programming contests are useful because you get a fairly clean signal: did the model solve the problem or not? But that’s a narrow slice of what we actually want these systems to do.

For software engineering, for example, you’d want to know whether a model can enter an unfamiliar codebase, understand an ambiguous request, make a change, test it, and respond to feedback. That’s much closer to useful work than solving a self-contained problem. And you need analogous evaluations in other domains, where success may require judgment, asking the right questions, or recognizing that you don’t have enough information.

As models become more capable, I think the unit of evaluation needs to shift from an individual answer to an entire task over time. Can the model sustain progress? Can it recover from mistakes? How much human supervision does it need? You also want to measure reliability, because succeeding once is very different from being something people can depend on.

So I’d want a portfolio of evaluations: controlled tests that help us understand specific capabilities, alongside realistic tasks that tell us whether those capabilities translate into useful outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response proposes realistic tasks and evaluations across domains, but does not specifically propose real-world research as an evaluation setting.

r002.rationale: It describes software engineering tasks in unfamiliar codebases, but does not identify coding coworking or testing whether models learn in high-context settings.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluating whole tasks over time, but does not identify coding coworking as a test of learning in real-world, long-horizon settings.

sol-6.1.text:
Programming contests are useful because you can check whether an answer is right, but they capture a pretty narrow slice of what we want these systems to do. In real work, the problem usually isn’t neatly specified. You have to figure out what matters, ask questions, use tools, and recover when something doesn’t work.

So I’d like to see evaluations move toward longer, more realistic tasks. Can a model take an ambiguous request and produce something a person actually finds useful? Can it work with someone over multiple iterations? And can it recognize when it doesn’t have enough information, rather than confidently pushing ahead?

We also need to measure reliability. A model succeeding once on a difficult task is exciting, but that’s different from being dependable enough that you can delegate that task to it. I think the evaluation question increasingly becomes: what can you trust this model to do, under what conditions, and how much oversight does it need?
